title: AI designs quantum programs, then has to prove they work

questions.q: Which of these are the variables in this program?
questions.explain: qubits, steps and cost all store values, and cost counts even though it is worked out from the others, while "Cost: " in quotes is just text.

questions.q: A new design is 4 times cheaper. What does the program display?
questions.explain: 12 × 50 is 600 and line 4 divides it by 4 to make 150, so it isn't 600 because cost is changed again before it is displayed.
SEND ... TO DISPLAY on line 4 shows something on the screen, while line 2 is input because it takes in what the user types.

questions.q: The proof checker types fail. What does the program display?
questions.explain: fail is not "pass", so only the ELSE branch runs, and it never shows both because IF ... ELSE picks just one path.

questions.q: What data type is stored in saving?
questions.explain: 2.5 has a decimal part, so it is a real number, and it isn't an integer because integers have no decimal part.

questions.q: How many times is "Checking proof" displayed?
questions.explain: REPEAT ... UNTIL always runs once before it checks the condition, so it displays once, not 0 times, even though tries > 0 is already TRUE.

questions.q: How many times is "Proof checked" displayed?
questions.explain: problems goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and only 3, 4 and 5 are more than 2, so it is 3 times, not 5, because the IF skips the first two.

questions.q: Should we accept this design? Is proof = "pass" AND cost <= 100 TRUE or FALSE?
questions.explain: The proof passed and 90 is less than or equal to 100, so both sides are TRUE and AND gives TRUE.
errors = 0 is TRUE, and NOT flips TRUE into FALSE.

questions.q: Is qubits < 1000 OR qubits > 5000 TRUE or FALSE?
questions.explain: 4374 is not below 1000 and not above 5000, so both sides are FALSE and OR gives FALSE.

questions.q: The AI suggests a program and a proof, and Lean says the proof fails. What is the next step in the algorithm?
options: Read the error and try again
questions.explain: The AI read the error and tried again until the proof passed, and quietly making the task easier was exactly what the separate check was there to stop.

questions.q: The team split the job into: choose a problem, write what the program must do, design it, prove it, check the proof. Which skill is that?
questions.explain: Breaking one big job into smaller steps is decomposition, while abstraction would mean leaving out details that don't matter.

questions.q: A design's cost must be from 1 to 1000. You test it with 500. What kind of test data is that?
questions.explain: 500 is safely inside the range, so it is normal data, while boundary data would be right at the edge, like 1 or 1000.

questions.q: Would you trust a program more if a strict computer had checked its proof?
options: Yes, a proof is better than tests
Only if people checked it too
No, I'd want to see it run
questions.explain: Talk about it: what can a proof show that 3 passing tests can't, and what could still go wrong?
